opus-5.5.text:
I think the thing that will be hardest for them to understand is how *normal* it all felt from the inside. If you look back at any exponential, whether it's COVID in early 2020 or compute scaling over the last decade, the curve looks obvious in hindsight. You plot it on a log scale, it's a straight line, and you think, "How could anyone have missed this?" But when you're living through it, each individual step looks incremental. A model gets a little better at coding, a little better at reasoning, it passes some benchmark that a year ago people said was years away, and everyone sort of absorbs it and moves on. The goalposts shift so smoothly that you never feel the ground moving under you.

I think historians will also struggle with the disconnect between what the people closest to the technology were saying and how the broader world was reacting. You had researchers, including people at my company and at others, saying fairly plainly, "We think systems that are as capable as top humans across most cognitive tasks could arrive within a few years." And that was often received as either hype or science fiction. Meanwhile, the public conversation was frequently about whether chatbots make silly mistakes, or whether this is a bubble, which are reasonable questions but somewhat orthogonal to the underlying trend. I think in retrospect people will find it strange that a claim that consequential could be made in public, repeatedly, by credible people, and not really be metabolized by institutions.

And honestly, I don't fully exempt myself. Even when you believe the curve intellectually, there's a part of your brain that keeps expecting tomorrow to look like today. You know the exponential is there, but you still make plans and have intuitions as though it isn't. So I think the hardest thing to convey will be that combination: the trend was visible, it was being talked about, and yet almost nobody, including the people who believed in it most, was emotionally or institutionally acting as though it was really happening.

r001.rationale: The response says exponential progress looks obvious in hindsight, while each step felt incremental and ordinary to people living through it, including those who intellectually believed the trend.

r002.rationale: It says researchers predicted top-human-level capabilities within a few years and that the public did not absorb the claim, but does not clearly convey that the public may remain unaware when transformative AI is only one or two years away.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the thing they'll struggle with most is how people could have had the data in front of them and still not believed it.

You know, I've had this experience for about a decade now. The scaling laws were visible in 2017, 2018, 2019. You could literally draw the line. And every year, I'd say to people, look, the line keeps going, and every year the reaction was essentially, well, sure, it's gotten better at this one thing, but it can't do X. And then a year later it could do X, and the goalposts would just quietly move to Y. Nobody ever said, I was wrong about the trend. They just found a new thing it couldn't do yet.

And I think historians will look back and find that genuinely puzzling, because in retrospect it'll look like the most obvious thing in the world. The curve was smooth. It wasn't hiding. It's a bit like, you imagine someone in 1995 looking at Moore's Law and saying, okay, but computers will never be able to do video. The error isn't a factual error, it's a failure to extrapolate from a trend that's been reliable for years.

Now, to be fair to people, I think there are a couple of reasons it was hard. One is that exponentials look flat for a long time and then they look vertical, and humans are just not wired for that. Our intuitions are linear. The second is that the systems at any given moment were always kind of embarrassing in some specific way. They'd write a beautiful essay and then fail at arithmetic. And people anchored on the embarrassing thing rather than on the rate of change. I'd say the rate of change was always the thing that mattered, and almost nobody looked at it.

The other thing I think will be hard to understand is the sort of cultural split. You had people inside the labs who were, frankly, quite alarmed, both excited and alarmed, and then you had a broader public and policy conversation that treated the whole thing as either hype or a toy. And those two groups were looking at the same models. I think historians will ask, how did the people closest to it and the people furthest from it reach such different conclusions, and why did it take so long for those to converge? Part of the answer is just that saying "this is going to be the most consequential technology in history" sounds like something a salesman says. So even when it was true, it got discounted as marketing. There's almost a boy-who-cried-wolf dynamic, except in this case the wolf kept showing up on schedule.

And then I'd add one more, which is a little self-critical. I think they'll be puzzled by how little we did with the time we had. Because if you believed the curve, you had years of warning. And a lot of the preparation, on safety, on policy, on economics, happened quite late, quite reactively. I'd like to think that's one of the things we're trying to change, but I don't want to pretend we've gotten it right.

r001.rationale: It says the trend will look obvious in hindsight and describes people’s disbelief at the time, but does not explain how hindsight obscures the uncertainty faced by people who bet on the trend.

r002.rationale: It says the broader public treated AI as hype or a toy, but does not say they might remain unaware even when transformative AI is only one or two years away.

astra-6.text:
I think they’ll struggle to understand how people could acknowledge the exponential intellectually and still be surprised by each successive step. And I don’t mean that as a criticism of other people. It’s hard for those of us working on it, too. You can look at a curve, you can extrapolate it, and then you go back to your day-to-day life, where things mostly feel the same.

There’s also a real difficulty in distinguishing between a system being impressive and a system being consequential. People try a model, notice something silly it gets wrong, and understandably use that to calibrate their expectations. But the question is how quickly those limitations are disappearing. A snapshot can be accurate and still give you a misleading picture of where things are going.

What I hope historians preserve is the uncertainty. Looking backward, whatever happened will look inevitable. Living through it, you have to work out which trends will continue, which bottlenecks matter, and when capabilities will translate into changes in the world. You can take the possibility of very rapid progress seriously without knowing exactly how it’s going to unfold.

r001.rationale: It says that looking backward, events will seem inevitable, while people living through them had to navigate uncertainty about trends, bottlenecks, and consequences.

r002.rationale: It does not say the public may be unaware of transformative AI arriving soon, or mention a one- or two-year timeframe.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’ll struggle to understand the gap between seeing the curve and really believing its implications. You could look at the progress, you could say, “Yes, this is exponential,” and then go back to making plans that implicitly assumed the world would stay roughly the same for another twenty years.

And I don’t think that’s necessarily stupidity. You experience the world one day at a time. The model gets better, but you still have to answer your email, you still have to get lunch. There isn’t some moment where the exponential announces itself and everyone updates their entire worldview.

The other thing is that the uncertainty was real. In retrospect, whatever happened will look inevitable. But while you’re living through it, you’re asking: Does the next generation keep improving? Does this particular limitation turn out to be fundamental? How long does it take for capability to translate into economic impact? Those are different questions, and you can be right about the overall trend and wrong about several of them.

So I suspect historians will find this strange combination of anticipation and normality. People discussing extraordinarily consequential possibilities, sometimes quite seriously, while the institutions around them continue operating on their usual schedules. From the inside, that combination feels much less strange than I think it will look from the outside.

r001.rationale: The response says that in retrospect events will look inevitable, while people living through them faced real uncertainty about continued progress, limitations, and economic impact.

r002.rationale: It describes people carrying on with normal routines despite discussing consequential possibilities, but does not say the general public may be unaware of transformative AI one or two years away.
